primary_meaning: In most Christian teaching, the west is understood as the direction of the setting sun and therefore symbolizes endings, completion, decline, or death — the close of day as opposed to the east's new beginning. It is very frequently invoked in tandem with the east to express totality or infinite distance, most famously in the assurance that God removes believers' sins 'as far as the east is from the west,' an immeasurable, unrepeatable distance signifying complete forgiveness. A closely related homiletical point notes that in the tabernacle and temple the entrance faced east and the Holy of Holies lay at the west end, so that movement westward pictured drawing nearer to God's presence, whereas movement eastward (as in the expulsion from Eden) pictured departure from Him.
primary_basis: Psalm 103:12 ('as far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us')
Psalm 113:3 ('from the rising of the sun to the place where it sets, the name of the LORD is to be praised')
Malachi 1:11 (God's name great among the nations 'from the rising to the setting of the sun')
Isaiah 43:5-6 (gathering offspring from the east and the west)
Isaiah 45:6 and Isaiah 59:19 (from the rising of the sun to the west, God's glory/name known and feared)
Matthew 8:11 / Luke 13:29 (many will come from east and west to sit at table in the kingdom)
Exodus 26-27 and Exodus 40 (tabernacle layout: entrance on the east, Most Holy Place at the west end)
Genesis 3:24 (cherubim placed at the east of Eden, implying expulsion was eastward, away from God's presence)

alternatives.meaning: West as one pole of a merism expressing totality or the whole world ('east and west' = everywhere), used of God's universal reign, the worldwide gathering of God's people, and the inclusion of the Gentiles rather than carrying an independent symbolic value of its own.

West as the direction of the sea (Hebrew 'yam,' the Mediterranean, is the standard Old Testament word for west), so that in Hebrew idiom the west is simply 'seaward' — a geographic rather than symbolic usage; some interpreters extend this to associate the west with the sea's connotations of chaos or the unknown.
basis: Numbers 34:6 (the Great Sea as the western border)

alternatives.meaning: West as the direction of decline, darkness, or death because the sun sets there — used in patristic and liturgical tradition, where baptismal candidates faced west to renounce Satan (the region of darkness) before turning east toward Christ, the rising Sun of Righteousness.
basis: Patristic baptismal liturgies (e.g., Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogical Catecheses; Ambrose, On the Mysteries) — a liturgical-traditional basis rather than a direct proof text
Malachi 4:2 and Luke 1:78 supply the contrasting eastern 'sunrise' imagery

alternatives.meaning: West as movement toward God's presence: because the sanctuary's Most Holy Place lay at the west end and Eden's exile was eastward, some teachers read westward movement as a picture of return, atonement, and approach to God (the priest moving west through the tabernacle furniture toward the mercy seat).
basis: Exodus 26:22 (the west end of the tabernacle, the rear where the ark stood)
Ezekiel 8:16 (sun worshipers facing east with backs to the temple, condemned)

alternatives.meaning: West as an eschatologically negative or judgment-associated direction in some strands of interpretation (e.g., the false sign in Matthew 24:27 where the true coming flashes from east to west, or later Jewish-Christian speculation associating the west with the nations/Rome).
basis: Hosea 11:10 (children trembling/coming from the west at the Lord's roar, read variously)

notes: Unlike 'east,' which carries a fairly recognizable symbolic profile in Christian interpretation (sunrise, Eden, the coming of Christ), 'west' has no single settled symbolic meaning in mainstream biblical scholarship. It functions most often (a) geographically, as 'seaward' in Hebrew idiom, and (b) rhetorically, as half of the east-west merism for totality or infinite distance (Psalm 103:12 being the most-preached text). The sunset/death/darkness association is strong in liturgical tradition (renunciation of Satan facing west) and in general religious symbolism, but it is applied to Scripture homiletically more than exegetically. The tabernacle-oriented 'westward toward God's presence' reading is popular in some devotional and typological teaching but is a minority position. Answers to 'what does the west symbolize in the Bible?' therefore vary considerably by tradition, and I have marked consensus as unsettled.
